title: Celebration-of-Life Concierge Using Restaurants' Dead Hours
one_liner: A flat-fee, turnkey memorial-gathering service for families who buy a cheap direct cremation and then have to improvise a goodbye, hosted in restaurants, breweries and hotel rooms during their empty weekday hours.
customer: Adult children (45-65) who bought direct cremation and must host 40-100 guests. Distribution partners are low-cost direct-cremation providers and hospice bereavement teams. Venues (restaurants, breweries, event rooms) pay a commission for filled dead hours.
problem: Funeral homes are hated for opaque upselling, so families flee to direct cremation at roughly $1,000-$3,000. That unbundles the ceremony: the gathering still happens 2-6 weeks later, but nobody provides it. Families scramble to find a venue, catering, a slideshow, an officiant and a livestream for remote relatives, while the cremation provider has no product for the moment that most shapes the family's memory of them.
solution: One booking that covers venue, per-head menu, host or officiant, memory-board and slideshow, RSVP and guest messaging, livestream and a printed program. The family pays a flat planning fee. The venue keeps the food and beverage revenue and pays a commission. Cremation providers and hospices embed a link in their after-care emails and take a referral fee or white-label it as their own add-on. A vetted list of local celebrants and photographers sits underneath.
why_now: The US cremation rate reached about 63.4% in 2025 and direct cremation is the fastest-growing disposition. NFDA reports that a majority of people have attended a funeral event at a non-traditional location, so the behavior has already shifted while the supply side is still a patchwork of ad hoc rentals. Restaurants and breweries are hunting for private-event revenue in weekday afternoons.
revenue_model: Family pays $750-$1,500 planning fee, plus add-ons (livestream, officiant, printed programs). Venue pays 12-15% of the food and beverage minimum (a 60-guest gathering at $55-$80 a head is $3-5k of spend). Referral fee of about $100 per booking to cremation providers and hospices.
non_obvious_insight: The funeral industry unbundled its own most emotional and highest-margin product. Disposition is now a commodity, but the ceremony did not disappear; it moved two to six weeks later, out of the funeral home, into a category no one owns, and it comes with a no-panic timeline, so the family is willing to plan and spend on it. The scarce resource is not a chapel, it is a trusted person who takes care of the whole afternoon.
first_30_days: Pick one high-cremation metro (Portland, Seattle, Las Vegas or Phoenix). Sign 8-10 venues with private rooms and per-head menus. Get two direct-cremation providers and two hospice bereavement coordinators to send a 'what happens next' link to families. Run the first gatherings by hand with a shared calendar, a phone line and a single landing page. The first paid bookings should come through partner referrals within weeks, and the service can stay fully concierge until 30-40 gatherings show what to automate.

title: Through-the-Package Drug Verification Library
one_liner: A subscription spectral fingerprint library and scan-on-receipt workflow that lets pharmacies and wholesalers verify what is actually in a sealed vial or blister pack, using off-the-shelf handheld Raman/NIR devices.
customer: 503A/503B compounding pharmacies and telehealth GLP-1 dispensers receiving vials or API from overseas, secondary wholesalers and repackagers, hospital pharmacies, and med-spa distributors.
problem: ARPA-H states that drug-related morbidity and mortality cost $528 billion per year, that recalls affect the medication of over 150 million Americans each year, that 'most recalls only happen after patients are exposed', and that only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports, a process that takes weeks. Serialization under DSCSA tracks the box (package-level identifiers, 24-hour notification of illegitimate product), not the molecule inside it, so a convincing counterfeit or diluted vial passes every paperwork check.
solution: Do not build hardware. Rent or resell existing handheld Raman/NIR units, and build the proprietary part: a reference library of authentic and adulterated finished-dose spectra measured through blisters, vials and prefilled pens, plus a classifier and a chain-of-custody report (photo, lot number, spectrum, pass/fail/uncertain). Uncertain results route to a partner lab for confirmatory HPLC. The library improves with every scan.
why_now: ARPA-H's FASTPASS program (solicitation ARPA-H-SOL-26-160; solution summaries due September 21, 2026, full proposals November 10, 2026) is funding through-packaging sensing (TA1 SAMPLE) and analytics (TA2 DETECT), which signals that the sensing hardware and spectroscopy science are mature enough to commercialize. GLP-1 volume and compounding have widened the exposure of small dispensers who have no way to check incoming product.
revenue_model: $1 to $3 per scan (usage SaaS), $300 per month device rental, $150 to $400 per escalated lab confirmation, and $6k to $24k per year library license for wholesalers.
non_obvious_insight: DSCSA verifies labels and traceability, not contents, and ARPA-H itself says the gap is one 'no single agency, manufacturer, or current technology can close alone'. That leaves room for a private data product. The moat is the library of through-package spectra, not the scanner, and it compounds with every customer scan. Evidence: https://arpa-h.gov/explore-funding/programs/fastpass ($528B, 150M Americans, 'only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports', TA1 SAMPLE and TA2 DETECT) and https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-supply-chain-integrity/drug-supply-chain-security-act-dscsa (package-level identification and 24-hour illegitimate-product notification). Caveat: the ARPA-H page did not give product types or counterfeit prevalence, and the GLP-1 exposure is my inference from public FDA alerts.
first_30_days: Pick 10 high-volume SKUs (injectable GLP-1 vials and pens plus a few high-value generics). Buy authentic references, make in-house dilution and wrong-API samples with a partner lab, rent two handhelds, and collect spectra through the packaging. Offer 3 compounding pharmacies and 2 regional wholesalers a free 30-day pilot with scan-on-receipt. Convert to paid on a per-scan plan. Skip the FASTPASS proposal unless a university partner handles it.

title: Data Centers That Make Water From Waste Heat
one_liner: Containerized membrane-distillation skids that use a liquid-cooled data center's own warm return loop to turn cooling-tower blowdown or brackish well water into clean make-up water.
customer: Colo and AI-hosting operators in Texas, Arizona and Nevada facing water audits, plus immersion-cooled bitcoin and HPC hosts whose loops run hot. Operators buy or lease; fabs later.
problem: Data centers are the target of water regulation (Texas freeze and reporting crime, Australian standards, New York and Ohio actions), and cooling blowdown creates a discharge headache. Desalination was uneconomic because heat was expensive, but a data center produces heat it must remove anyway.
solution: Integrate membrane-distillation modules from an existing OEM with the site's warm loop (liquid-cooled racks now return water at roughly 45-65 C, my estimate). The skid concentrates blowdown and produces distillate for make-up water, cutting purchased water and discharge volume. Add a metering-and-ledger layer that produces a verified 'water-negative' claim. First product: a 10-50 m3/day skid.
why_now: A 2025 Chinese plant reported desal near $0.28/m3 using waste heat (not fully verified). Liquid cooling is spreading, and regulators and lenders now ask for verified water use.
revenue_model: $250-600k equipment sale per skid, or water-as-a-service at roughly $1.5-3/m3 plus O&M. Regulatory value (fewer permits, less discharge) is the closing argument.
non_obvious_insight: Membrane distillation lost to reverse osmosis because it needs large amounts of heat, and a data center offers abundant heat that must be removed, so its energy cost is effectively negative. The villain of the water story becomes the equipment that solves it.
first_30_days: Find three immersion-cooled mining or HPC hosts in Texas with 55-65 C loops. Partner with an MD module OEM for a 5 m3/day trial unit ($60-120k). Sign an LOI with a host for a 90-day pilot that shares data on kWh-thermal per m3, TDS and fouling.

title: Retrain Displaced Managers for Data-Center Builds
one_liner: A 10-week bridge program that turns laid-off program managers, analysts and ops leads into project-controls, cost-estimating, commissioning-paperwork and permitting roles at data-center and grid builders.
customer: General contractors, EPC firms, data-center developers and utility contractors pay a $12-25k placement fee or staff-augmentation margin. Learners pay little, or the cost is covered by workforce-board funds.
problem: Everyone tells displaced office workers to 'learn AI', the most crowded direction. Meanwhile AI's own physical build-out has a shortage of schedulers (P6), cost engineers, document controllers, commissioning coordinators and interconnection or permit analysts. Contractors can't hire them, and mid-career office workers face 6-13 month searches.
solution: Cohort training on scheduling, cost control, contracts, commissioning documentation and site-safety basics, taught by retired project-controls leads. It includes a paid 4-week job-shadow on live projects, certification prep (OSHA 30, PMI-SP, AACE) and guaranteed interviews with partner contractors.
why_now: Hyperscaler capex on data centers and grid work is at record levels and contractors openly cite labor shortages. Big-company cuts of managers ('anti-bureaucracy' layoffs like Amazon's ~16,000) are pushing experienced coordinators onto the market. Stanford data shows the pain concentrated in AI-exposed office roles.
revenue_model: Placement fee of 10-15% of first-year salary (about $12-18k) from contractors, plus paid corporate cohorts and optional deferred tuition.
non_obvious_insight: The AI boom creates a shortage of non-technical, non-AI office roles in the physical world. The displaced manager's scarce skill (vendor wrangling, org navigation, documentation discipline) is exactly what construction lacks, and nobody is training for it.
first_30_days: Call 20 mid-size mechanical and electrical contractors in hot markets (Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Arizona) and get their unfilled-role lists. Sign 3 pay-per-hire LOIs. Recruit 15 laid-off PMs from layoff communities. Run a 4-week evening pilot with a retired scheduler and place the first 5.

title: Toll Fermentation in Dead Alt-Protein Plants
one_liner: Buy or lease bankrupt alt-protein bioreactor capacity for pennies and run it as a toll fermenter for whey-alternative brands.
customer: Precision-fermentation whey and casein brands at Series A/B stage, plus protein buyers who need non-dairy supply.
problem: More than 70 alt-protein companies have merged or shut since Sept 2024, leaving idle fermentation assets, while whey is sold out and brands like Verley have product and FDA clearance but not plant capacity.
solution: Acquire or option distressed fermenters and downstream-processing lines, retool them into a multi-tenant toll plant, and sign take-or-pay reservations with whey-alternative brands.
why_now: H1 2026 alt-protein funding was only $197M (of which $132M fermentation), assets are cheap, and whey concentrate is up 108% in two years with buyers shifting from ESG goals to supply-risk mitigation.
revenue_model: Toll fee per kg processed plus take-or-pay capacity reservation fees; asset purchase is financed by anchor-tenant contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The sector's collapse is a capacity bargain arriving exactly when demand for non-dairy protein flipped from a values purchase to a supply-security purchase. The assets are worth more to a toll operator than to their bankrupt owners.
first_30_days: Catalogue stranded plants through bankruptcy brokers and lender sale lists, get LOIs from 2-3 whey-alternative brands for reserved capacity, and take a purchase or lease option on one plant contingent on an anchor contract.

title: Legal Price Bargaining Co-ops for Salmon Fleets
one_liner: Back-office software and staff that let independent salmon boats negotiate price as one bloc under the 1934 Fishermen's Collective Marketing Act, as the Bering Sea crab fleet already does.
customer: Member-owned fishermen's associations, starting with one district of 150-400 permit holders that sells to only 1-3 buyers (a Kodiak, Chignik, Cook Inlet, Prince William Sound or Southeast group, not Bristol Bay first). The association pays us. Its dues are collected as a small settlement deduction, about 0.25-0.5% of landed value.
problem: A salmon fisherman is a price-taker. The processor posts a base price and a bonus schedule in June, the boat delivers before it knows the final price, and the retros show up months later. Bristol Bay's average ex-vessel price went from $1.03 in 2025 to $1.72 in 2026, and 2026's $260M fishery came off only 30.1M fish. Nobody on the fishing side of that swing had a seat at the table. Meanwhile most skippers believe acting together is illegal price fixing, so the bar talk about a tie-up dies every spring.
solution: A compliance-first toolkit for member-owned associations. It includes counsel-reviewed charter and bylaw templates under 15 U.S.C. 521-22 and CFEC permit verification at sign-up. Members can vote by SMS. A firewalled clean team collects member-submitted price, volume and quality data. From that it builds a formula price tied to public benchmarks (wholesale frozen sockeye quotes, roe prices, yen and euro, canned prices) plus a quality bonus schedule. We supply the negotiators, contract templates (multi-year formula price, settlement deadlines, audit rights) and dues collection through settlement deductions. The association is the bargaining party and we are the vendor, so we never bargain or set prices ourselves.
why_now: The 2025 crash and 2026 rebound showed the fleet how much money moves on one posted number. Processors now compete with loyalty and quality bonuses (for example $0.15 for RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling). Bonuses are a formula, and formulas can be negotiated. Cheap e-sign, SMS voting and LLM contract review make an association nearly free to run. The crab fleet's Alaska Marketing Association proves the model works in Alaska.
revenue_model: $2-5K/month retainer per association, or 10-15% of dues. On a $260M fishery, 0.25% dues is about $650K/year, so a full-district association is a $65-100K/year account. Later add multi-association benchmarking subscriptions and negotiation-support fees tied to price gains.
non_obvious_insight: The FCMA has let fishermen, not processors, bargain collectively since 1934. The fear that bargaining equals price fixing comes from the DOJ case where processors were the defendants (Pan Alaska Fisheries). Associations fail on operations, not law: no clean data, no dues collection, no fast votes, no credible fallback. Outsiders assume the fleet lacks leverage, but what it lacks is a secretary's office with software.
first_30_days: Pay an antitrust and fisheries lawyer $10-15K for a 10-page FCMA playbook. Pick one small port with a near-monopsony buyer and hold 10 harbor and Facebook-group sessions. Get 30-50 permit holders to sign a non-binding letter of intent. Run a members-only survey of what each boat was actually paid, timed for settlement season (Oct-Dec). Publish a 'your fleet vs. the benchmark' report. Aim for one association signed at a $2K/month retainer by February, before prices post in late spring.

title: Carrier Watchtower: Insurer Failure Alerts for Lenders
one_liner: Early-warning scores on the thinly capitalized insurers behind mortgage collateral, sold to servicers before the next carrier failure.
customer: Mortgage subservicers, credit unions, community banks and MSR investors with Florida, Louisiana, California and Texas collateral.
problem: Insiders treat Florida as fixed because Citizens fell from 936K to about 395K policies. But take-out carriers got Citizens' data to cherry-pick policies. A CBS investigation (unverified detail) alleges owners of a receiving carrier diverted millions. Howden warns reinsurer returns may fall below cost of capital by 2027, so any reversal hits the retail layer first. If a carrier fails, thousands of loans lose hazard cover at once and servicers must force-place at multiples.
solution: Loan tape in, exposure out. Map each loan's insurer from insurance-tracking data to a live stress score built from statutory filings, reinsurance program renewals, assumed-policy concentration, complaint ratios, rating actions and regulator orders. Give a 90-day warning and a pre-negotiated replacement placement lane.
why_now: Florida's rapid depopulation of Citizens in 2025-26 moved risk onto newer, thinner balance sheets. Reinsurance is at record capital and softening now, and the margin squeeze is forecast for 2027.
revenue_model: SaaS priced at basis points or cents per loan per year, plus per-policy replacement placement fees.
non_obvious_insight: Analysts watch carrier surplus and lenders watch loans, but nobody joins the two. Rating agencies lag, and the soft market hides the fragility.
first_30_days: Build dossiers on the top 40 Florida carriers from public regulator filings. Sell a $5K exposure report to two credit unions or subservicers showing what share of their book sits with the weakest carriers.

title: Rent-a-Robot Creature Actors for Haunts and Events
one_liner: A rental troupe of costumed quadruped and humanoid robots, with operators and safety systems, for haunted attractions, festivals, conventions and immersive shows.
customer: Haunted attractions, seasonal theme-park events, festivals and conventions, immersive theatre producers and brand activations.
problem: Haunts struggle to hire and retain actors, and scares repeat. Fans love character robots (Disney's droids), but building one is expensive and risky, so small producers cannot offer them.
solution: Buy off-the-shelf sub-$5k quadrupeds and $6-16k humanoids and fit them with fabricated creature shells. Add a director's tablet for scripted and remote-driven behaviors, geofencing and e-stops, and insurance. Rent at $800-2,500 per night with an operator.
why_now: Cheap quadrupeds and humanoids with open-source locomotion are available, entertainment robots are already common in China, and Halloween is five weeks away.
revenue_model: Nightly rental plus operator fee, then creature shell and kit sales and character licensing.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part is not the robot, it is the show: safety envelope, character design, logistics and insurance. Amortizing hardware over 100+ nights a year makes this a creature-troupe service business, not a robotics company.
first_30_days: Lease 2 robots for about $6k and build two creature shells. Book 3-5 haunts and one convention for October and November at about $1,000 per night. Get event insurance and a written safety protocol.

title: WhatsApp Tandas With Credit Reporting
one_liner: Felix proved WhatsApp-native finance at $8B of volume. Wrap the rotating savings groups that immigrant households already run in group chats with escrow, default cover and credit reporting.
customer: Latino, West African, Caribbean and South Asian households running tandas, susus and chit-fund-style rotating savings groups. The FDIC's 2023 survey counts 5.6M unbanked and 19M underbanked households, with minimum balances the top barrier.
problem: Rotating savings groups are the real financial system for many households, but they run on cash and trust, one bad organizer or defaulter breaks the pot, and the on-time payment history is invisible to credit bureaus. Cash-funded remittances now carry a 1% federal tax, nudging cash economies toward digital.
solution: A WhatsApp bot to create a tanda (amounts, order, schedule). Contributions are held in a partner-bank pass-through balance, or in stablecoin where appropriate, and payouts release on schedule. The organizer earns a fee, and a small guarantee pool covers late payers. On-time contributions are reported to bureaus as installment history through a furnisher partner.
why_now: Felix reached $8B cumulative volume with revenue up 2.5x on WhatsApp, the remittance tax pushes cash users to digital rails (Forbes, 2026-07-17), and stablecoin and bank-partner rails make small-balance escrow cheap.
revenue_model: 1-2% fee on each pot, $5 per month credit-building subscription, and lender referral fees for graduated members.
non_obvious_insight: Don't replace the tanda, wrap it. The organizer is a trusted social underwriter with better default data than any bureau. The pooled payment history of organized groups becomes a proprietary dataset lenders will pay for.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 organizers via Spanish-language WhatsApp and Facebook groups, churches, taquerias and community organizations. Run 10 pilot tandas with manual escrow in a partner-bank sub-account at a 1.5% fee, and validate the credit-reporting path with a furnisher.

title: Court-Ready Smoke Testing Protocol for Fire Survivors
one_liner: A standardized smoke and ash sampling protocol plus lab network that satisfies California's new smoke-damage presumption law, sold to public adjusters, policyholders and eventually carriers.
customer: Public adjusters, policyholder attorneys and restoration contractors handling open LA and Southern California fire claims, paying $1,200-3,500 per home. Carriers and TPAs are a later channel, since the law makes testing an insurer-funded cost.
problem: Fire survivors have fought carriers for months or years over whether smoke-contaminated homes are safe. There is no agreed testing or restoration standard, so each claim becomes a fight between competing consultants. The new law shifts testing cost to insurers and blocks Additional Living Expense from ending until homes are restored and safe.
solution: A published sampling protocol and chain-of-custody workflow run by certified industrial hygienists and partner labs. It produces a report format mapped to the statute's language (presumption, testing funded by insurers, pre-loss restoration). We bundle software that generates the sampling plan, tracks lab results, and drafts the repair scope. Sell to public adjusters first, then offer carriers a neutral-standard option.
why_now: AB 1795 was signed on 2026-09-15 and introduces a smoke-damage presumption, insurer-paid testing and sampling, inspection and claims-handling timelines, and adjuster training. The industry group APCIA asked that guidance be 'grounded in credible science, valid methodologies.' SB 876, signed 2026-09-28 and effective 2027-01-01, doubles penalties for unfair claims practices during declared emergencies and requires insurers to file disaster recovery plans, raising the stakes on slow claims.
revenue_model: Per-home testing and reporting fee of $1,200-3,500. Software seats for public adjusters at $200-400 per month. Later a per-claim neutral-testing fee from carriers and TPAs, and lab partnership revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The law creates a paid testing mandate without naming a standard, so whoever defines the accepted protocol captures the spend. Evidence: https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/west/2026/09/15/885209.htm (presumption, insurer-paid testing, ALE protections; APCIA's 'credible science' quote; contentious smoke claims after the 2025 LA fires) and https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/release031-2026.cfm (Commissioner Lara: families 'have spent months, and sometimes years, fighting over whether their homes were safe'). https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release034-2026.cfm covers SB 876, including doubled penalties in emergencies and a 15-day adjuster-change update. Public adjusters have no neutral, repeatable science kit today, and carriers lose in disputes when their own hired consultant is the only standard.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 certified industrial hygienists and 1 accredited lab in the LA area. Draft the protocol from published standards and the statute text. Offer 10 public adjusters with open Eaton and Palisades claims a discounted first three homes in exchange for case studies. Invite APCIA member claim managers to review the protocol for credibility.

title: Worker-Ownership Succession for Home Care Agencies
one_liner: A specialist shop that helps retiring home-care agency owners sell to their caregivers via an ESOP or worker co-op, plus a shared back office for the converted agencies.
customer: Owners aged 58-72 of $2-15M revenue home-care agencies with no successor. CDFI lenders and employee-ownership funds are financing partners.
problem: Reimbursement is squeezed (a 1.3% aggregate cut for CY2026, with a -3.0% temporary adjustment still in place), private-equity money goes to software and big platforms, and even UnitedHealth had to divest 164 Amedisys locations. Small owners have no buyer, while agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year.
solution: A conversion shop: valuation, readiness (licensure and payer change-of-ownership rules), structure (S-corp ESOP, worker co-op or employee-ownership trust), financing (seller note plus CDFI or SBA), and a two-year ownership-culture program (caregiver equity, profit sharing, scheduling voice). Converted agencies share a back office (payroll, billing, EVV, recruiting).
why_now: Boomer owners are retiring into a weak sales market after the 2026 rate squeeze, and the workforce shortage means the workforce is the scarcest asset. Cooperative Home Care Associates in the Bronx shows the model works.
revenue_model: Transaction fee of 3-5% of deal value, $8-15k a month back-office fees, and a small share of network EBITDA.
non_obvious_insight: In a business where turnover is the profit killer, the best buyer for a struggling agency is the workforce itself. Ownership is a retention tool, and the exit-plan angle sells to owners who don't care about culture.
first_30_days: Work with a state home-care association to get 20 owner conversations. Sell five $12k ownership-readiness assessments, line up a CDFI lender, and target first LOI within six months.

title: Rescue Monitoring for Orphaned Home Solar
one_liner: An installer-agnostic gateway plus subscription that watches home solar systems whose installer went bankrupt, produces warranty-ready evidence, and dispatches a vetted local electrician.
customer: Homeowners with installer-abandoned solar systems (owned or financed). B2B: solar loan servicers and asset managers holding loans and leases from failed installers, who care about collateral performance. Local electricians and solar technicians are the fulfillment network.
problem: Installers such as Sunnova (Chapter 11 in June 2025, roughly 500,000 customers) and others collapsed. Systems keep running, but nobody is watching or servicing them. Silent faults (failed optimizers, tripped rapid shutdown, inverter errors) can cost months of production. Warranty claims require documentation the homeowner doesn't have, and installer apps degrade or vanish.
solution: A gateway that reads inverter data locally (SunSpec Modbus and local APIs) plus a CT clamp on the main panel. It compares actual output to modeled output using open weather and irradiance data, classifies probable fault types (string, inverter, shading, curtailment), and generates a warranty evidence pack for the equipment manufacturers. A flat-fee price sheet dispatches vetted local technicians. Start with the three or four most common inverter families.
why_now: The installer failure wave (SunPower in 2024, Sunnova in 2025, many smaller firms) is producing large orphaned fleets. The federal residential solar tax credit ended for expenditures after 2025, so more installers will exit and fewer new ones will absorb the orphans. Gateways and cloud analytics are now cheap.
revenue_model: USD 8-12 per month plus a USD 150-250 gateway or a USD 199 'solar health check plus 12 months' bundle. Dispatch margin of 15-20% on repairs. B2B data-and-triage feed of USD 2-4 per system per month for servicers with 10k+ systems.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing isn't data, because the inverter clouds still exist. It's someone accountable who reads the data and moves a truck. Sell a primary-care doctor for a solar system with a referral network. Lenders care because a non-producing system correlates with default, which gives a second payer.
first_30_days: Recruit orphan-solar homeowners through r/solar and Facebook groups. Ship 50 gateways to owners of two or three inverter families. Sign 3-5 electricians in Texas, California, Arizona or Florida on a fixed price sheet. Sell the health-check bundle and use the first detected faults as marketing proof. Approach two loan servicers with the aggregate underperformance findings.

title: Paid Neighbor Walking Routes for Absent Kids
one_liner: Hire retired neighbors and parents as paid 'route captains' who walk or wake up chronically absent kids on fixed blocks, and get paid a share of the funding that the recovered attendance brings back.
customer: Principals and districts in states that fund schools on average daily attendance (California, Texas and similar). Secondary payers are city safe-passage budgets, Title I funds and Medicaid plans (for asthma and chronic-condition kids).
problem: About one in four kids is chronically absent. Nudge letters and text campaigns work on the 10 to 19 day group but barely touch the kids missing 25 or more days. For them it is a 7:40 a.m. logistics problem: a parent working an early shift, an older sibling who moved on to middle school, a dangerous corner, no clean clothes, no alarm clock. In attendance-funded states, each absent day costs the school roughly what a day of instruction is worth, so a $200-per-kid fix pays back several times over.
solution: Micro-employ 3 to 5 route captains per school as part-time W-2 workers (7:00 to 8:30 a.m., roughly $18 an hour). Each captain covers a block-by-block route, walking 6 to 10 kids, knocking on doors, and running a breakfast and laundry pass. Captains report barrier codes by voice note, which feed the attendance team's dashboard. Contract as a base route fee plus 20 to 25 percent of documented funding gains from improved attendance.
why_now: Chronic absenteeism has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. ESSER-funded attendance staff were cut as that money expired. States now require chronic-absence plans, and the retiree and gig-worker labor pool is looking for short, local, part-time work.
revenue_model: Base fee per route plus a performance share of recovered attendance funding. Optional per-route sponsorship from health plans or employers.
non_obvious_insight: Districts spend on software and letters, but the students who cost the most are the ones for whom the 7:40 a.m. logistics fail. The cheapest fix is a grandmother on the corner, and it is invisible to edtech buyers because it is not a product. The first three Mondays of September predict the year, so contracting has to start before October.
first_30_days: Pilot with one principal in an attendance-funded state: 2 routes, about 12 kids, 4 part-time captains recruited from churches and senior centers. Establish baselines from last year's attendance data and track days present weekly. Write the performance addendum as a one-page contract that a principal can sign with discretionary funds and later convert to a district contract.

title: Receipts-Only Reviews via Open Banking
one_liner: Reviews that only people who provably paid can post, with the payment verified through open-banking data and only merchant, amount band and month disclosed.
customer: UK and EU independent restaurants, salons, tradespeople and clinics (verified-review widget and profile subscription), with lenders, insurers and marketplaces as later data buyers.
problem: Trustpilot removed 4.5M fake reviews in 2024 and was fined by Italy in Mar 2026 for failing to verify authenticity. The FTC rule and UK consumer law ban fake reviews, and no platform can verify offline purchases. Merchants cannot prove their reviews are real, and review sites sell services to the businesses they rate.
solution: The reviewer links a bank through an open-banking account-information partner (such as TrueLayer or GoCardless). The app reads one transaction and produces a selective-disclosure attestation (merchant, amount band, month), then posts. Merchants get a '100% paid-customer reviews' widget and structured-data markup. Reviewers get neutral, sentiment-independent cashback funded by merchants.
why_now: Fake-review enforcement is intensifying (FTC warning letters Dec 2025, Italy's Trustpilot fine Mar 2026), the AI-generated review flood is growing, and AI shopping agents ingest reviews as trust signals. Open banking now has enough UK users to make linking a normal action.
revenue_model: GBP 19-49 per month merchant subscription, API and data licences to lenders and marketplaces, and float on cashback funding.
non_obvious_insight: The referee problem vanishes when the proof comes from the bank, not the platform. A review site that sells to the businesses it rates can never be trusted, but a receipt cannot be bought.
first_30_days: Sign 30 independent restaurants in one UK city, put a QR code at the till, and build on an open-banking partner's sandbox. Launch with local press as 'the review site you cannot buy'.

title: Passive Elder Wellness Checks From Water Flow
one_liner: A daily 'your parent used water normally' text built from a clip-on flow sensor or a utility's smart-meter feed, sold to adult children as flood protection first and wellness second.
customer: Adult-child caregivers of solo-living 75+ parents and early-dementia patients (about $14/month), resold through home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging. Secondary buyers are water utilities with interval (AMI) meters that want a customer-care program.
problem: Wearables get abandoned, cameras get refused, and 69% of adults 50+ are uncomfortable sharing health data with AI tools. Yet 27% of Americans 65+ live alone, 59M family caregivers work unpaid, and agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year. China's 'Are You Dead?' check-in app topping paid charts in Jan 2026 shows families will pay for the thinnest possible 'are they OK' signal.
solution: A clip-on flow sensor on the main line, or opt-in utility interval data, plus fixture-signature disaggregation, learns each home's routine (first morning tap, flushes, showers, kitchen). It alerts on no morning use by a set hour, repeated 3 a.m. flushes (wandering), a tap left running, a sudden drop in showers (an early hygiene and dementia marker) and scald-level hot water. An optional auto-shutoff valve stops floods. The family gets a daily 'all normal' text, with an escalation tree to family, then the agency, then a welfare check.
why_now: Drought pressure has pushed utilities to roll out interval meters and customer portals for leak detection, so the data already exists. Medicaid cuts (about $911B) and shrinking Medicare Advantage benefits push more seniors onto unpaid family care. Older-adult tech acceptance is rising (23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, up from 10%). The 2026 China check-in app proved mass demand for minimalist check-ins.
revenue_model: $14/month per home plus a $79 kit. Agencies pay $6 per client per month for white-label. Utilities pay a license or revenue share of roughly $0.25-0.50 per enrolled account per month once AMI opt-in works.
non_obvious_insight: Water is the one utility no person can skip, fake or forget to charge, and no eldercare company sells it. It sidesteps the privacy and compliance objections that kill cameras and wearables. The 'leak and flood protection' pitch lets a proud parent accept something they would refuse as 'monitoring'. Japan's kettle-based 'mimamori' watch-over services showed appliance-use check-ins work, and water is the version that scales on utility infrastructure.
first_30_days: Buy 100 off-the-shelf clip-on flow monitors. Pitch three local home-care agencies and two caregiver Facebook groups a '$99 parent flood-and-check-in kit', and ship 50. Build the routine-anomaly model on consented data over 60-90 days. Then offer one small AMI-equipped utility an opt-in pilot using interval data.

title: Seller-Financing Rails for Paid-Off Homeowners
one_liner: A compliant seller-carry-in-a-box that lets free-and-clear homeowners become the bank, with underwriting, servicing, tax packaging and a note-sale exit.
customer: Retiring owners with paid-off homes and large embedded gains (SF, Chicago and other coastal markets), their listing agents and attorneys, and buyers who cannot or will not take a 7.5% bank loan (self-employed, thin-file, relocating).
problem: 30-year rates are about 7.4-7.6%, 58% more sellers than buyers and 42.5% of listings have price cuts, so deals die on financing. About 40% of owner-occupied homes carry no mortgage, and their owners could earn a better yield than deposits while deferring capital-gains tax through an installment sale. Today seller-carry is a handshake plus a lawyer, with no underwriting, servicing or exit, and federal and state rules on ability-to-repay and balloons make DIY risky.
solution: A packaged workflow: buyer ability-to-repay underwriting, state-specific note and deed-of-trust documents, a licensed sub-servicer with tax and insurance escrow, installment-sale tax packets, and a standing bid to buy the note when the seller wants liquidity. Agents get a listing-side toggle, 'seller-carry available', that widens the buyer pool.
why_now: Record buyer's market with rising rates makes sellers' cheapest concession their own balance sheet. Futures now price a 5% Fed funds rate by end-2027, which makes note yields attractive, and AI document and underwriting tooling makes small-loan servicing economical.
revenue_model: 1-1.5% origination fee paid by the buyer, $25-35 per month servicing, a 1-2 point spread on note sales, and an agent subscription tier.
non_obvious_insight: The best 'rate buydown' is not paying points to a bank but becoming the bank. Free-and-clear boomers hold the largest un-deployed lending balance sheet in housing and are one compliance product away from using it. Sellers with gains above the primary-residence exclusion also get a tax reason to spread proceeds over years.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a workable seller-finance framework and partner with a licensed originator and servicer there. Recruit 30 listing agents from local groups. Sell a $499 flat seller-carry consult to 10 sellers and track how many close. Have counsel sign off on the federal seller-financing exemption conditions before any live deal.

title: Clickwrap Gatekeeper: Agents Buy Contract Counsel
one_liner: An API agents call before clicking 'I agree'. It returns clause-level risk against the principal's delegated-authority policy, plus a signed archive of exactly what was accepted.
customer: Wallet-holding consumer and enterprise agents, and the platforms that run them, paying $0.02-$0.50 per document evaluation plus an evidence-archive fee per acceptance. Agent-wallet and browser-agent vendors are the natural embedders.
problem: Agents will accept tens of thousands of ToS, DPAs, auto-renewals, arbitration waivers and data-resale clauses for people and companies. Courts increasingly treat automated assent as binding, so the open legal question is the scope of the agent's authority. Agents can read a contract, but none has a legal-grade policy engine or a defensible evidence trail. Amazon's fight with Perplexity over agent access is one visible example of that unsettled authority.
solution: check(url_or_text, policy) diffs the document, hash-cached and versioned, against the principal's policy: max liability, no auto-renew beyond 30 days, no mandatory arbitration, no resale of personal data. It returns ALLOW, ESCALATE or REFUSE with cited clauses. On ALLOW it snapshots the page (hash, timestamp, screenshot) into a tamper-evident log so the principal can later prove what was accepted. A diff feed alerts the principal when terms change on services already accepted. It is positioned as a policy engine, not legal advice, with law-firm-authored policy packs.
why_now: Agent authority is the live legal question of 2026, with law-firm memos on 'authority to bind' and litigation over agent access. Payment protocols such as AP2 mandates and ACP mean agents now click through payment terms without a human present. Browser agents are in production use.
revenue_model: Metered evaluation (first-seen documents priced high, cache hits nearly free), an evidence-archive fee per accepted contract, enterprise policy packs, and a marketplace for lawyer-written policy templates with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The unit of legal risk in the agent economy is not the model's hallucination but the tiny irrevocable assent. Because most ToS are near-identical templates, one shared cache amortizes legal analysis across millions of agents, which no single company can do for itself. Lawyers become policy authors rather than reviewers, and gross margin exceeds 90% once the cache is warm.
first_30_days: Crawl and index ToS, privacy and DPA pages for the top 5,000 SaaS and e-commerce sites and cluster them into templates. Publish a free MCP server with 1,000 free checks. Recruit 3 advisory lawyers to seed policy templates. Pitch agent-wallet startups and browser-agent vendors to embed it as a pre-payment check, and start charging in month 2.

title: Waze for Agents: Live Bureaucracy Route Data
one_liner: A pay-per-lookup feed of the current, tested state of consumer and government web procedures (form changes, outages, hidden requirements, real step timings), sold to browser agents just before they attempt an errand.
customer: Browser and computer-use agents, and the agent platforms that run them, paying $0.005-$0.10 per route lookup via x402 or MPP. The heaviest users will be agents doing errands: license renewals, permits, benefits applications, insurance claims, utility transfers, refunds.
problem: Procedure websites change weekly with no changelog. Every failed attempt burns tokens, and worse, can leave a half-finished irreversible state such as a submitted but unpaid renewal. Every agent relearns the same breakages, and nobody pools that knowledge.
solution: Two data engines. First, synthetic canaries: daily automated dry-runs of the top ~500 US flows (state DMV and DOL, county property tax, SSA/IRS/USCIS account setup, top utilities, top insurers' claim portals, airline refund forms). They record schema diffs, required documents, CAPTCHAs, session timeouts and upload limits, and publish step-by-step 'route cards' with a success rate and freshness timestamp. Second, opt-in failure telemetry from customer agents, traded for credits, which covers the long tail Waze-style. Customers get a 'route guarantee': if a route verified in the last 24 hours fails, the lookup is refunded.
why_now: Browser agents moved from demo to production in 2026, with vendors reporting thousands of automated workflows per week on legacy portals. x402 and MPP make $0.01 lookups collectable without accounts. Governments are still not publishing agent-readable metadata.
revenue_model: Metered lookups, plus $500-$5,000/month platform plans for agent vendors that include telemetry credits. Premium verified-fresh routes for high-stakes flows, and later aggregate breakage analytics sold to agencies who want to fix their own forms.
non_obvious_insight: For an agent the scarce input is not information but freshness plus negative results: knowing what broke this morning. Agents' own failures are the raw material, so each new customer improves the map, a data network effect a static scraper cannot copy. Government sites are the one part of the web nobody will ever optimize for agents, which keeps the drift problem permanent.
first_30_days: Write 50 Playwright canaries for the 10 highest-traffic flows in 5 large states, using a cheap model to diff DOM and field schemas. Publish a free MCP server and a public 'status page for bureaucracy' to draw agent builders. Offer free credits to 5 browser-agent startups in exchange for telemetry, and start charging in month 3 once the route guarantee has a track record.

title: Point-in-Time Certification for Alternative Data Vendors
one_liner: A vendor-paid, buyer-trusted forensic test that a dataset's history is genuinely point-in-time, extended to certify that an LLM-driven signal isn't leaking hindsight, plus a cheap timestamp 'witness' service.
customer: Mid-sized alt-data vendors and AI-signal startups ($2M to $50M ARR) selling to funds, at $15K to $40K per certification, about $8K per year to recertify, and $500 per month for the witness service. Fund data-sourcing teams use the reports free, which is what makes the badge valuable.
problem: Quants ask every vendor one question: 'when did you start collecting live?' The honest answer is usually that the history was reconstructed, with today's entity maps and taxonomies, overwritten revisions, and publication timestamps standing in for availability timestamps. Funds burn three to six months of trials before discovering this. Vendors lose deals, and every fund duplicates the same diligence. LLM signals add parametric hindsight, where the model's weights already know the outcomes of the backtest period.
solution: A standardized battery run on vendor samples under NDA. It tests for discontinuities at the claimed live date (coverage, missingness, revision rates, distribution shifts, entity-map consistency, timestamp-lag distribution) and for survivorship and delisting gaps. For LLM signals it runs black-box hindsight probes and entity-masked or post-cutoff re-runs. The output is a PIT Grade, a one-page badge and a machine-readable report. The witness service takes a daily cryptographic hash or snapshot of the vendor's feed, so in a year the vendor has third-party-provable live history.
why_now: Thousands of data vendors now sell into funds, banks and AI-agent builders who lack quant-grade diligence. 2025 to 2026 research (Look-Ahead-Bench, HindsightBench, detecting lookahead in LLM forecasts) has made LLM look-ahead bias a mainstream worry. Regulators are scrutinizing hypothetical and backtested performance claims.
revenue_model: Issuer-pays certification fees, annual recertification, a per-month witness subscription, and a premium hindsight audit for AI-signal vendors and allocators diligencing AI-driven funds.
non_obvious_insight: The only real proof of point-in-time history is a third party's timestamps, because vendor engineers routinely overwrite and backfill. Each buyer rediscovers this privately, so the cost is duplicated across hundreds of funds. Shifting the cost to the vendor, who wants the shorter sales cycle, is the arbitrage. Credibility requires published methodology and public aggregate fail rates, or it becomes a pay-for-grade scheme like pre-2008 ratings.
first_30_days: Open-source the PIT test suite on GitHub and publish teardowns of three public datasets. Get two or three fund data-sourcing heads to say they would use the reports. Sell five vendors a $7.5K 'pre-audit' in exchange for being named references, and launch the witness hash service to any vendor who asks.

title: Satellite Cannibalization Scores for Rural ISP Lenders
one_liner: Address-level risk scores that show which rural ISP portfolios LEO broadband will hollow out, and which it will not.
customer: Lenders to rural ISPs (cooperative and agricultural lenders, community banks), funds buying wireless or fiber ISPs, tower and fixed-wireless investors, and state broadband offices that allocate subsidies.
problem: Starlink went from 8.9M to 12M subscribers in six months (per the briefing) while ARPU fell 19% in one quarter. That means it is pricing down into the rural segments small ISPs live on. Lenders still underwrite these ISPs on legacy subscriber-count assumptions, and nobody can tell which locations are actually exposed.
solution: A data product that scores every serviceable location: fiber or cable alternatives, fixed wireless, LEO availability and price, local congestion, and expected churn or ARPU pressure. It rolls up to portfolio covenants, valuation adjustments and acquisition due-diligence reports. Updated monthly as satellite pricing and capacity change.
why_now: Subscriber growth of about 35% in six months, falling ARPU and satellite eligibility in subsidy programs all landed in 2025-26. Starship-driven capacity growth should push prices down further.
revenue_model: Portfolio subscription $2-10k per month per lender. $10-40k per acquisition due-diligence report. Data licensing to ISP-focused funds.
non_obvious_insight: The consensus is fiber wins and satellites lose. The actual exposure is mid-density fixed-wireless and DSL footprints, and the difference is visible at address level. Lenders get paid for knowing which side of that line each loan sits on.
first_30_days: Build a prototype on public availability maps, FCC broadband data and published Starlink plan tiers for three states. Pitch five agricultural or community lenders with a free look at one real portfolio. Convert one to a paid pilot.

title: Slop-Risk Diligence for Creator-Business Buyers
one_liner: A fixed-price quality-of-earnings report that prices the platform-policy cliff hiding inside a YouTube channel, newsletter or podcast network for sale.
customer: Search funds, micro-PE roll-ups, creator funds and revenue-based lenders acquiring channels, newsletters and podcast networks priced at roughly $200k-10M, and the brokers who sell them.
problem: Buyers price trailing-12-month revenue. But YouTube's Jul 16 clarification demonetizes generic or repetitive content and AI personas on finance, legal and health topics, Snap stopped recommending fully-AI content, and LinkedIn added a slop-report button. A channel can look healthy on the last year's statements and be one policy update from losing its income. Traditional QoE providers and listing brokers do not model this risk.
solution: A five-day diligence package: audit of how content is produced (share of AI scripts, voices and visuals, template repetition measured via embeddings, reused and stock footage), a policy-risk score against current platform rules, revenue concentration, copycat and re-post exposure, strike and claim history, and an 'earnings at risk' range with suggested earn-out triggers. Templated pipeline with analyst review.
why_now: Creator M&A and creator funds are growing (Slow Ventures' $60M creator fund, brokered channel sales), and the July 2026 policy clarifications make the next 12 months structurally different from the last 12.
revenue_model: $2.5-7.5k per report (roughly 1% of deal size), fund subscriptions for 10+ reports a year, and $500/month post-close earn-out monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Diligence prices the past, and the AI-slop rules make the coming year differ from the past one. Policy risk is a new line in an existing budget, so no new budget is needed.
first_30_days: Pull 50 public listings from Flippa, Empire Flippers and Acquire. Publish five free teardowns, then sell $2.5k reports to buyer communities and search-fund Slack groups.

title: Fast-Pay Administrator for Funded Home Repair
one_liner: Run the paperwork and pay small contractors in days on grant- and program-funded repairs (weatherization, aging-in-place, municipal repair programs) where waitlists exist because few pros will bid.
customer: Nonprofits, community action agencies, Area Agencies on Aging, housing authorities and municipal home-repair programs with budgets but weak execution capacity.
problem: Programs have money but not throughput: jobs are small ($2-15K), paperwork-heavy (income verification, lead-safe rules, photos, inspections) and reimbursed in 30-90 days. Good contractors are too busy for low-margin, slow-pay work. The median home is 44 years old, repair-over-replace is at 62%, and homeowners cannot get quotes.
solution: Act as general contractor of record plus payment desk: take the program's approved scope, match it to vetted small pros, run documentation and inspections in a phone workflow, pay the pro in 5-7 days by fronting cash, and bill the agency with audit-ready files. The agency's program-delivery budget line pays the admin fee.
why_now: Aging housing stock and record remodeling spend ($524B) mean small pros have plenty of alternatives to slow-pay work. Vision and document models make photo-based compliance cheap. Slower remodeling growth (about 1.6% by year-end) should free some pro capacity for steady program work.
revenue_model: 12-18% admin fee on job value paid by the agency, plus a 1-2% factoring spread on advances.
non_obvious_insight: In public repair programs the scarce input is neither money nor eligible homeowners, it is good contractors' willingness to endure paperwork and slow pay. Fast payment plus document automation is the moat, and the customer already has a budget line for program delivery.
first_30_days: Approach five agencies with waitlists in one state. Offer a 10-job cost-plus pilot. Recruit 10 small pros on a 7-day-pay promise. Open a $75K working-capital line and run documentation through simple phone forms.

title: Vet-Supervised Cattle Crews for the Screwworm Era
one_liner: Custom-harvester-style crews do the 80% of a vet's working day that is labor (inspect, treat navels, tag, record) so the scarce vet supervises and signs instead of holding the chute.
customer: Ranchers in screwworm zones and buffer states (Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma) paying per head or per day; sale barns, stocker operations and feedlots that need pre-movement inspection documentation; and overloaded rural vet practices that subcontract overflow to a crew.
problem: Only about 1.3% of vets work in food animal practice, and South Texas vets say it will not be physically possible to handle every screwworm case. Daily inspection is the core control, newborn calves' navels are prime targets (past outbreaks saw navel strike rates as high as 50% in unprotected calves), and ranchers with 300-3,000 head across brush country do not have the labor to look at every animal every day.
solution: A vet-supervised service company (a rural vet as medical director, or a vet-owned entity) fielding 3-4 person crews with a trailer: portable squeeze chute, EID reader, wound-care kit, vet-approved treatment protocols, and a photo- and GPS-stamped inspection log that the vet countersigns. The seasonal product is an 'NWS Season Program' of scheduled pasture rounds, navel treatment on newborn calves, wound checks, prescribed prophylactic treatments under an existing VCPR, and movement paperwork. Off-season the same crews run preg-checks, weaning, vaccination and processing days year-round, with the vet doing exams and sign-off.
why_now: The first US screwworm detections came in Texas in June 2026, followed by more counties, a New Mexico detection, and the first infested horse in September. Sterile fly supply is constrained, federal and state agencies have imposed movement restrictions and mandatory veterinary inspections in affected areas, and FDA has moved to authorize treatment products. Spring calving in Texas is the next high-risk window.
revenue_model: $3-8 per head per treatment or round, day rates around $1,800-2,500 per crew for working days, seasonal retainer contracts, and a 20-30% margin on subcontracted overflow from vet practices. Target roughly 35-40% gross margin per crew.
non_obvious_insight: The vet shortage is largely a labor-allocation problem: a $250-per-hour license is spent on tasks that only need hands. Custom crews are normal for harvest, hay and branding, but herd health stayed in-house because vets never delegated it formally. Practice-of-veterinary-medicine laws let a supervising vet delegate many tasks, and once the vet is medical director of record the boundary is workable. The durable asset is the trained crew that keeps earning long after screwworm fades, because labor-short ranches will keep buying it.
first_30_days: Sign 2 overloaded vets in Texas or New Mexico as medical directors, and confirm what each state's practice act allows non-vets to do. Buy a used portable chute, trailer and 2 EID readers (about $15K), recruit 3 experienced ranch hands or vet-tech students, and get liability coverage. Sell 5 ranches a fall program of weaning-time inspections and navel and wound checks on fall-calving herds, then sell the spring calving program from the results.

title: Physical-Properties Index for Every SKU
one_liner: A shared 'Gracenote for grasping': weight, center of mass, deformability, best grip points and packaging traits for millions of SKUs, sold to pick-robot makers and brands.
customer: Pick-and-pack robot vendors, 3PLs running robotic induction, CPG and retail brands (for robot-ready packaging certification), and humanoid developers.
problem: Picking robots fail on the long tail because they meet every SKU cold, and brands change packaging without notice. Amazon knows internally, but everyone else relearns per site.
solution: Fill the index from two sources: a scanning rig at partner 3PLs (3D scan, mass, center of mass, slip tests) and give-to-get contributions from robot fleets reporting grasp outcomes. Serve it by GTIN through an API with recommended grasp points and packing advice, and offer brands a 'Robot-Ready' grade that 3PLs reward with lower handling fees.
why_now: Robotic picking is now at scale (Amazon 1M+ robots, Symbotic $2.25B revenue, Maven-style mixed palletizing), and foundation models can use priors like these. A market of data buyers already exists.
revenue_model: API fees per lookup or per robot per month, $2-10k per SKU family for brand certification, and dataset licensing to model labs.
non_obvious_insight: Robots will not scale on smarter grasping alone. The world's goods need a machine-readable physical spec, and brands have a direct incentive because 3PLs and retailers will reward robot-ready packaging. A neutral index can become a standard the way GS1 barcodes did.
first_30_days: Build a $15k scanning rig at a friendly 3PL and scan the top 3,000 SKUs. Release a free tier, sign 2 pick-robot vendors as beta partners, and run one paid brand packaging audit.

title: A Private IRIS for States and Utilities
one_liner: A consortium of former EPA toxicologists that sells open, peer-reviewed health-risk assessments (nitrate, PFAS mixtures) to state agencies, utilities, insurers and courts.
customer: State environment and health agencies (multi-state membership), large utilities, pollution-liability insurers, state attorneys general, litigation counsel and muni-bond analysts. Agencies and utilities pay membership, and lawyers and insurers pay per project.
problem: Step one: EPA's Office of Research and Development, home of IRIS, was eliminated in 2026, and the nitrate cancer review has stalled since 2023. Step two: EPA cannot update hazard values, while the four PFAS limits proposed for rescission (PFHxS, PFNA, GenX and the Hazard Index) may leave states to decide. Step three: states, utilities, insurers and courts need citable, transparent assessments to set or defend limits, and no one supplies them.
solution: A 'systematic review desk' using pre-registered protocols, external peer review and open publication. First deliverables: a nitrate health assessment and a PFAS mixture assessment, each with a state-adoptable guidance value and a cost-benefit table. Sell expert testimony and state-specific screening levels as add-ons.
why_now: ORD's elimination has released a talent pool of experienced risk assessors at the same moment the PFAS proposals are in comment and the nitrate review is stalled. The 2026 rollback creates a patchwork of state standards.
revenue_model: Consortium membership of $75-250k/yr per state or utility group, $150-500k per assessment, and expert-witness fees.
non_obvious_insight: Government risk-assessment capacity is a public good that is now for sale, and the asset is credibility, not technology. The buyers exist because states, insurers and courts need someone defensible to cite. Independence (open protocols, multi-funder, no client-directed conclusions) is the product.
first_30_days: Recruit three to five ex-ORD or IRIS scientists and incorporate as a public-benefit corporation. Pre-register a nitrate protocol. File an independent analysis in the open EPA PFAS docket to build credibility. Pitch three state agencies and the state drinking-water administrators' association.
